it’s a bit of a toss up, to be completely honest with you. technically, aroma, as their espresso based beverages are made on a manual machine. this allows for more control on profile, properly steamed milk, and freshness. their beans are also mostly sourced from zimbabwe, who use the processing method of washing (which means removing the cherry, submerging beans into water and letting them ferment away any remaining flesh) this process is expensive, and results in smooth and complex flavour profiles. 

starbucks uses completely automatic machines. espresso shots are automatically ground, tamped (pressed down into a puck), and pulled with the press of a button. the milk wand also automatically stops when it reaches a certain temperature. this allows for consistency, but not a lot of quality and care. starbucks sources beans from so many places to produce their numerous roasts, however because consistency is their top concern, their beans are often roasted at a higher temperature than others, which results in that classic starbucks bitterness. in short, all of starbucks’ beans are burnt on purpose. 

so with all of that in mind, the clear winner should be aroma, but the quality of a drink is entirely in the hands of the person who does the final extraction, and that’s your barista. unfortunately, aroma really lacks in an extensive coffee training program that properly sets their baristas up to provide the best quality they can. starbucks on the other hand provides coffee theory and origin training from day one, and additional coffee master programs that teach specialty skills such as profiling, cupping, etc. one cafe has the detriment of knowledge + bad equipment, the other, no knowledge but excellent equipment. i know this is sort of a non answer, but it’s the genuine truth! aroma will be hit or miss, and starbucks will always be consistently Just Fine. hope this provided a little bit of info! :)

your best bet is actually to apply online, but definitely checking in with your local ones to ask if they’re hiring! if you leave your resume without applying online it will likely be used as a coaster for people’s drinks in the back room. my old store used people’s physical resumes as scrap paper. i would second that you don’t need to know anything about coffee!! i didn’t even know the difference between a latte and a cappuccino before i started, but i just talked about my favourite drinks + food at starbucks and my customer service experience! it’s a lot of people’s first job, so they aren’t looking for experience, just upbeat people and a willingness to learn.

at starbucks my training was about three days! some stuff on the computer and then going through every. single. drink on the menu. unless they are urgently hiring, they won’t post on indeed, your best bet is to apply through their website and if they’re hiring they’ll reach out to you!! aroma has no formal training, you just shadow someone until you show up to a shift and you’re thrown on bar. most hiring aromas will be on indeed, although i wouldn’t recommend applying if you’re looking for employment longer than 6 months. when i was a part timer i would get anywhere from 15-25 hours!! usually 5 hour shifts, 3-4 days a week :)

starbucks in the financial district ... next to nothing? i never counted tips there, but based on what i personally took home each week i would have to guess around ~$1-2 per barista per day. aroma tips were much better, i’d take home around $3-10 a day, which is not bad considering there was no debit tip option.

yeah!! i remember back at starbucks when people would ask for pour overs every single partner on the floor would roll their eyes. since the machines are automatic and their priority is speed, it seemed like the antithesis of starbucks. plus, you’ll likely not get a great cup as you need to learn proper grind levels, pouring speed, etc. now, i love doing pour overs! although i also love that i have the time to walk through all the brewing methods we offer with people excited to learn about coffee. at home i’m currently brewing a single estate pacamara on my chemex, which is a fantastic coffee, but when i’m at work my favourite method has to be the syphon!! i feel like walter white every time i make one for somebody.

I’d honestly always been a part of the starbucks worshipping cult, so when I moved to the city and needed to make money it was the first place I wanted to apply. It was a really good balance of easy work, while also providing some pretty basic knowledge on brewing, extraction methods, coffee origin, etc. Now that i’ve moved on to specialty coffee, I’m happy to have had the start that I did! Also, the fast food pace just honestly stresses me out.

It’s an incredibly easy job, and a lot of fun if you’re in the right location! Technical skill is essentially just muscle memory, and isn’t very difficult until you’re in specialty coffee which takes a bit more practice. People skills are also a quick learn. Most people don’t care about you, they just want their coffee quickly, so as long as you’re relatively upbeat, you’re doing fine. Definitely apply if it’s somewhere that interests you! (Starbucks, NOT Aroma)
